My colleague reminds me that this type of housing should be available not only in big cities such as Montreal and Toronto, but also in small towns and villages.
We think the government should participate more fully in public housing by increasing the mortgage ratio from the present 75-25 per cent ratio to a 90-10 per cent ratio. This recommendation was made by representatives at the federal-provincial conference. It is about time that the minister took immediate action to solve the problem of public housing. One cannot expect a municipality to participate on the basis of a ratio of 75-25 per cent. Not only is the ratio too high but they have other requirements, such as building schools and recreational and other facilities. We also feel that the public housing subsidy should be tied to income rather than to the present formula of 50-50.
The present 75-25 per cent ratio to a 90-10 per cent ratio.
We would also encourage, Mr. Speaker, massive purchases of land. This was a recommendation made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in his statement to the federal-provincial conference. This action must be taken by federal and provincial governments in order to bring down the high cost of land.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we would also increase home improvement loans. The record of home improvement loans in the last few years indicates that these loans have been declining. The reason has been that people have not felt inclined to borrow money from the banks under the Home Improvement Loans Act. It may be that some arrangement could be made with the municipalities whereby home owners borrow money for improvement purposes and add the repayments to their tax payments each year. It is fairly obvious that under the present home improvement scheme, with the banks administering and financing the land, things have not worked. I suggest the minister give close study to some arrangement between the
National Housing Act
municipalities and the government under which money made available to the municipalities could be lent to home owners to improve their homes, the repayments being added to their tax.
These are some of the corrective measures that we would take, Mr. Speaker. We hope the "band-aid approach" of the new minister will be altered and that he will apply his mind and his energy to solving the critical housing shortage in Canada. If he does, he will probably make a name for himself in the cabinet and across the country. If he does not, then the minister will fall into the political wastebasket that so many other cabinet ministers have fallen into when it comes to solving the housing crisis in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like also to say a few words about that bill which I support with some reluctance, without however being against an increase in the loans made or guaranteed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I feel that this increase to $18,000 was needed, because houses costs more and more to build and rents keep going up.
In my opinion, it is mostly for that reason that the minister agreed to introduce that amendment to the National Housing Act, but at the same time that justifies the criticism directed at the present government in the last few years by the Canadian public, the contractors and the eventual homeowners.
We notice a steady increase in the cost of houses, building materials and, consequently, rents. Housing is the main factor responsible for the increase in the price index, in the cost of living index. We have just completed a debate on that subject, and the rise in the cost of living has forced the government to take a position which, in my opinion, will not solve the problem. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) saw no other solution to fight inflation, and the increase in the cost of construction comes precisely into that price index which compels the government to take action and stabilize prices.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I should like to analyse briefly the causes that contributed to rent increases.
One of the most important is precisely that 11 per cent tax on building materials which seems even more significant than it appears. When an individual has a house built or purchases materials to improve the one he

March 8. 1968
National Housing Act
already owns, in most cases, he has to get a mortgage from an approved lender of the Central Mortage and Housing Corporation. He must also borrow the 11 per cent tax on building materials for his house. Now, the interest on that loan has reached 8J per cent. This also means that the individual who decides to make repairs to his house will have to pay during 25 or 30 years an interest of 81 per cent on the 11 per cent levied on building materials.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
There is also another important fact and those who live in Quebec are aware of it. We also have in the province of Quebec an 8 per cent sales tax which is added to the federal tax, because it is computed when the amount of the federal tax of 11 per cent has been established. This means a 20 or 21 per cent tax on building materials on which an individual will have to pay 8| per cent interest. Therefore, this is a scandalous item which increases considerably the cost of housing. I contend that, by removing that tax as was done a few years ago, we would considerably reduce the cost of housing and the minister would not have to put before us this amendment to-day.
In housing, the increase of municipal taxes, and mainly school taxes, must also be taken into consideration. As far as the province of Quebec is concerned-I do not know exactly what happens in the other provinces-school taxes increase at a rapid pace and there is no way of stopping it, at least at the present time. Taxes increase the cost of housing and prevent the average wage-earners from becoming homeowners. Some have made great sacrifices to make the down payment on the purchase of a house; they have paid their monthly instalments during a few years and if they are out of work for the shortest period on account of sickness, accident or other circumstances, they find themselves in an unbearable situation, and they are often forced to give back the house for which they have remitted $8,000, $15,000 or $20,000, because they cannot meet their payments.
Mr. Speaker, as I see it, we have the right to expect from the government a better housing policy, because it is becoming increasingly difficult for those in the middle income bracket to purchase a home. That is why many people are undecided when the time comes to decide whether they should purchase a home or resign themselves to living in accommodation that belongs to others. One

wonders if they are not right in deciding to continue renting, because homeowners, in addition to what I mentioned a while ago, must take fire coverage and pay premiums which keep growing from year to year, and also attend to the maintenance of the house, to keep it in good condition.
And so, one realizes that today it is almost as costly to own a home as to rent one.
I think that the minister and the government should consider ordering as soon as possible a complete revision of the National Housing Act, for the benefit of both owners and tenants.
This amendment to the present act will certainly help some potential owners by allowing them to borrow more money, since the price of houses is going up. But even this will not solve their problems, far from it. It is perhaps a temporary solution but, sooner or later, these people will encounter even greater difficulties.
I admit frankly, Mr. Speaker, that I will vote in favour of the amendment proposed in the present bill.
I would have much preferred the minister responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to suggest another way to make things easier for those who want to own their home.

speechtext:
I shall detain the house for only a few moments because I do not consider that this simple amendment is a
National Housing Act
suitable occasion for a long speech on housing. We agree with the proposal which stipulates an increase in the amount available for mortgages and we shall support the move in this direction. I should like to leave one or two thoughts with the minister. I think it is time we all came to the conclusion, as we in the Social Credit party did many years ago, that financing in connection with housing should not be in competition with financing for industry. Industry can pass on its finance charges to the consumer, and this being the case it is in a much better position to bargain for finance than are people building houses. The purchaser of a home is simply buying a bill of expenses from the time he does so until he disposes of it. The home owner is therefore at a distinct disadvantage.
Surely we should reach the conclusion very quickly that funds for housing ought to be quite separate from any funds available to industry. In recognition of the special position of home owners and the value of home ownership, British Columbia many years ago instituted a home owners grant. It started out as a very small sum, $25 I believe for each home owner. Today it is $120-$130, my hon. friend tells me. The first $130 of an individual home owners taxes are paid by the provincial government.
It would be wise, in my view, to take the position adopted by the Social Credit party before the committee on banking and finance back in 1954, and set up a proper revolving fund to handle the needs of the housing industry. I think this would go a long way toward solving our housing problems. The money should be made available to home owners at the cost of operating the account and there should be no relation whatever between the interest rate charged and the rate charged for commercial loans. We believe the account could be handled with a rate in the neighbourhood of 2| per cent. Not only would we have a fund operating at a low interest rate, but we would be in the happy position of administering a fund which remained at a constant figure.
We have seen interest rates rise to astronomical heights-and not one more house has been built as a result. May I urge the government and the minister to take a good look at the possibility of setting up a revolving fund which would not be in competition with industry and which would be operated at the cost of handling the account quite distinct from prevailing commercial interest rates.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to indicate that this idea has not been abandoned; but I have not been the minister responsible for housing for too long a period of time. This is one of the things I have been considering with the officials of C.M.H.C. and with my advisers.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE RATIOS FOR INSURED LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister spoke about not wanting to make detailed calculations on how this legislation would apply to specific cases, and we can appreciate this. However, I think it should be pointed out that although additional moneys will help substantially to improve the housing situation, the average citizen will still encounter difficulty in view of current high interest rates.
Payment of interest and principal on a $14,000 loan over a 25 year period at 6 per cent would be $89.85 monthly, which is a reasonable payment for accommodation. At 7 per cent this rises to $98.06. At 8 per cent it rises to $106.85, and at 9 per cent, which is the rate at which we are selling money at present, it rises to $115.92, which in many cases is more than 25 per cent of a person's income.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE RATIOS FOR INSURED LOANS
speechtext: I wish to ask another question concerning limited dividend housing. I think it is pretty well known that limited dividend housing fell on its head because of certain indiscreet acts by the private sector a few years ago, whereby these projects were abandoned because private individuals tried to maximize their profits through various nefarious means. Has the minister anything to offer which will guarantee that the same situation will not happen again?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE RATIOS FOR INSURED LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are looking very carefully at the applicants for limited divided housing construction. We are trying to assure in every way that the C.M.H.C. can be certain there will be none of this business of building a limited dividend project, getting your profit out, and leaving it. We will do our utmost to avoid this, and my officials assure me that they believe they can avoid it under present circumstances.
